## Why I’d Sell Simon Property Group at US$182

[Simon Property Group shares are overvalued.](https://valuationbot.ai/blog/why-i-d-sell-simon-property-group-at-us-182) At US$182 a share, the market bakes in faster growth, fatter margins, and a longer runway than I think the assets can deliver. My base‑case value is US$152 per share, which points to 12–22% downside from here, so I would sell.

## **Investment thesis**

Simon Property Group is priced for perfection. At US$182 a share, the market bakes in faster growth, fatter margins, and a longer runway than I think the assets can deliver. My base‑case value is US$152 per share, which points to 12–22% downside from here.

The gap starts with what today’s price implies. To justify this level, you need roughly 5.2% revenue growth, a 44.7% long‑run net margin, and an 11‑year glide path to stability. I assume 4.5% growth, a 39% steady‑state margin, and ten years to stability. The difference may look small on paper, but over a decade it compounds into a large value gap.

The operational ceiling is already in sight. Occupancy sits near 96%, which limits scope for a step‑change in rent growth. Base minimum rent runs at about US$59 per square foot and escalators add steady, not explosive, uplift. Meanwhile, property operating costs and taxes keep grinding higher, which crimps the scope for margin expansion from here. On the current footprint, that mix points to mid‑single‑digit growth and a net margin that settles closer to 39% than 45%.

Unit economics back this up. Management’s own data imply operating costs around US$10.60 per square foot per year and an NOI margin in the low 60s—healthy, but hardly the stuff of further operating‑leverage miracles. When a portfolio is this mature, the heavy lifting comes from lease roll‑over and redevelopment, not from squeezing more out of day‑to‑day operations.

Duration is the other over‑reach. The shares embed an 11‑year runway; I think most large projects will be substantially stabilised by 2026, which argues for a shorter, ten‑year path back to steady state. A shorter runway lowers duration premia in any sensible model and trims fair value.

My DCF tells a consistent story. The base case lands at US$152 per share. Simulated outcomes cluster tightly: the 25th to 75th percentiles sit between US$142 and US$161, and even the 90th and 95th percentiles—US$170 and US$176—sit below today’s price. When your upside cases fail to clear the screen price, the burden of proof is on the bull.

Market multiples corroborate the caution. Retail REITs trade above mid‑cycle averages, and SPG itself sits rich on several measures: about 24.9× earnings (69th percentile), 10.0× sales (72nd), and 19.2× book (90th). Price‑to‑book is less helpful here given historic‑cost accounting, but a reasonable reset to roughly 21× earnings and 8.5× sales triangulates to US$145–US$160—a range that chimes with the DCF.

Two near‑term checkpoints could close the gap between hope and reality. First, full‑year 2025 results and 2026 guidance, expected in late February 2026, should anchor growth nearer 4.5% and margins around 39%. If that happens, I expect the market to take the premium down a notch, consistent with a move toward the mid‑US$160s to high‑US$150s. Second, redevelopment milestones through 2026 should confirm earlier stabilisation, which shortens duration and chips away at valuation support.

Of course, there are ways I could be wrong on the downside. Stronger leasing spreads, faster project stabilisation, or a lower discount rate would lift fair value. If growth trends closer to 5.2% and margins toward 44–45%, I could justify values from the high US$170s to high US$190s, which would challenge a Sell call. The bear case runs the other way: slower leasing, more dilution from international ventures, and a more capital‑intensive pipeline push value down toward US$113.

What will I watch? Three things. First, leasing spreads and the volume of leased‑but‑not‑open space; the former signals pricing power, the latter the pace to cash. Second, property‑tax and utilities lines; if they cool, margin pressure eases. Third, the cadence and returns of redevelopments and international JVs; that is where real upside could emerge if execution beats history.

Stepping back, Simon is a superb franchise with prime centres, sticky tenants, and an investment‑grade balance sheet. None of that is in doubt. The issue is the price. From US$182, the shares assume more growth, more margin, and more time than I can underwrite. Until guidance and milestones reset expectations, I see better risk‑reward elsewhere. I will avoid over the next 12 months and revisit after the 2026 outlook is on the table.

* ### Dividend yield above industry average

  Simon Property Group Inc., based in Indianapolis, is a retail REIT that is one of the largest owners of high-end malls, outlet centers, and lifestyle destinations in North America, Asia, and Europe. In 2016, the company had expanded its profile by investing in the retail operations of several well-known retail brands, including Reebok, Aeropostale, Nautica, and Forever 21 through its partnerships, including SPARC and ABG. The investments were reconsidered after the pandemic, once consumers began to return to outdoor retail spaces. In 2023, the company began to sell its interest in retail brands and in 2024, Simon sold its remaining interest in ABG brands. The company still has active joint venture interests including an 84% interest in the Taubman Group, a 22% interest in Klepierre, a Paris-based real estate firm, and SPARC. SPG also operates Simon Brand Ventures, which offers appraisals and real estate services.

## Why I’d Sell Simon Property Group at US$182

[Simon Property Group shares are overvalued.](https://valuationbot.ai/blog/why-i-d-sell-simon-property-group-at-us-182) At US$182 a share, the market bakes in faster growth, fatter margins, and a longer runway than I think the assets can deliver. ## **Investment thesis**

Simon Property Group is priced for perfection. At US$182 a share, the market bakes in faster growth, fatter margins, and a longer runway than I think the assets can deliver. My base‑case value is US$152 per share, which points to 12–22% downside from here.

The gap starts with what today’s price implies. To justify this level, you need roughly 5.2% revenue growth, a 44.7% long‑run net margin, and an 11‑year glide path to stability. I assume 4.5% growth, a 39% steady‑state margin, and ten years to stability. The difference may look small on paper, but over a decade it compounds into a large value gap.

The operational ceiling is already in sight. Occupancy sits near 96%, which limits scope for a step‑change in rent growth. Base minimum rent runs at about US$59 per square foot and escalators add steady, not explosive, uplift. Meanwhile, property operating costs and taxes keep grinding higher, which crimps the scope for margin expansion from here. On the current footprint, that mix points to mid‑single‑digit growth and a net margin that settles closer to 39% than 45%.

Unit economics back this up. Management’s own data imply operating costs around US$10.60 per square foot per year and an NOI margin in the low 60s—healthy, but hardly the stuff of further operating‑leverage miracles. When a portfolio is this mature, the heavy lifting comes from lease roll‑over and redevelopment, not from squeezing more out of day‑to‑day operations.

Duration is the other over‑reach. The shares embed an 11‑year runway; I think most large projects will be substantially stabilised by 2026, which argues for a shorter, ten‑year path back to steady state. A shorter runway lowers duration premia in any sensible model and trims fair value.

My DCF tells a consistent story. The base case lands at US$152 per share. Simulated outcomes cluster tightly: the 25th to 75th percentiles sit between US$142 and US$161, and even the 90th and 95th percentiles—US$170 and US$176—sit below today’s price. When your upside cases fail to clear the screen price, the burden of proof is on the bull.

Market multiples corroborate the caution. Retail REITs trade above mid‑cycle averages, and SPG itself sits rich on several measures: about 24.9× earnings (69th percentile), 10.0× sales (72nd), and 19.2× book (90th). Price‑to‑book is less helpful here given historic‑cost accounting, but a reasonable reset to roughly 21× earnings and 8.5× sales triangulates to US$145–US$160—a range that chimes with the DCF.

Two near‑term checkpoints could close the gap between hope and reality. First, full‑year 2025 results and 2026 guidance, expected in late February 2026, should anchor growth nearer 4.5% and margins around 39%. If that happens, I expect the market to take the premium down a notch, consistent with a move toward the mid‑US$160s to high‑US$150s. Second, redevelopment milestones through 2026 should confirm earlier stabilisation, which shortens duration and chips away at valuation support.

Of course, there are ways I could be wrong on the downside. Stronger leasing spreads, faster project stabilisation, or a lower discount rate would lift fair value. If growth trends closer to 5.2% and margins toward 44–45%, I could justify values from the high US$170s to high US$190s, which would challenge a Sell call. The bear case runs the other way: slower leasing, more dilution from international ventures, and a more capital‑intensive pipeline push value down toward US$113.

What will I watch? Three things. First, leasing spreads and the volume of leased‑but‑not‑open space; the former signals pricing power, the latter the pace to cash. Second, property‑tax and utilities lines; if they cool, margin pressure eases. Third, the cadence and returns of redevelopments and international JVs; that is where real upside could emerge if execution beats history.

Stepping back, Simon is a superb franchise with prime centres, sticky tenants, and an investment‑grade balance sheet. None of that is in doubt. The issue is the price. From US$182, the shares assume more growth, more margin, and more time than I can underwrite. Until guidance and milestones reset expectations, I see better risk‑reward elsewhere. I will avoid over the next 12 months and revisit after the 2026 outlook is on the table.

* ### Dividend yield above industry average

  Simon Property Group Inc., based in Indianapolis, is a retail REIT that is one of the largest owners of high-end malls, outlet centers, and lifestyle destinations in North America, Asia, and Europe. In 2016, the company had expanded its profile by investing in the retail operations of several well-known retail brands, including Reebok, Aeropostale, Nautica, and Forever 21 through its partnerships, including SPARC and ABG. The investments were reconsidered after the pandemic, once consumers began to return to outdoor retail spaces. In 2023, the company began to sell its interest in retail brands and in 2024, Simon sold its remaining interest in ABG brands. The company still has active joint venture interests including an 84% interest in the Taubman Group, a 22% interest in Klepierre, a Paris-based real estate firm, and SPARC. SPG also operates Simon Brand Ventures, which offers appraisals and real estate services.
  At the end of 2024, Simon owned or had interests in about 233 properties with about 12 million square feet of international leasable space and 170 million square feet of domestic space. Of domestic NOI, over 40% is from properties in portfolio-heavy Texas, California, and Florida. The REIT has a varied tenant base. ## **Investment thesis**

Simon Property Group is priced for perfection. At US$182 a share, the market bakes in faster growth, fatter margins, and a longer runway than I think the assets can deliver. My base‑case value is US$152 per share, which points to 12–22% downside from here.

The gap starts with what today’s price implies. To justify this level, you need roughly 5.2% revenue growth, a 44.7% long‑run net margin, and an 11‑year glide path to stability. I assume 4.5% growth, a 39% steady‑state margin, and ten years to stability. The difference may look small on paper, but over a decade it compounds into a large value gap.

The operational ceiling is already in sight. Occupancy sits near 96%, which limits scope for a step‑change in rent growth. Base minimum rent runs at about US$59 per square foot and escalators add steady, not explosive, uplift. Meanwhile, property operating costs and taxes keep grinding higher, which crimps the scope for margin expansion from here. On the current footprint, that mix points to mid‑single‑digit growth and a net margin that settles closer to 39% than 45%.

Unit economics back this up. Management’s own data imply operating costs around US$10.60 per square foot per year and an NOI margin in the low 60s—healthy, but hardly the stuff of further operating‑leverage miracles. When a portfolio is this mature, the heavy lifting comes from lease roll‑over and redevelopment, not from squeezing more out of day‑to‑day operations.

Duration is the other over‑reach. The shares embed an 11‑year runway; I think most large projects will be substantially stabilised by 2026, which argues for a shorter, ten‑year path back to steady state. A shorter runway lowers duration premia in any sensible model and trims fair value.

My DCF tells a consistent story. The base case lands at US$152 per share. Simulated outcomes cluster tightly: the 25th to 75th percentiles sit between US$142 and US$161, and even the 90th and 95th percentiles—US$170 and US$176—sit below today’s price. When your upside cases fail to clear the screen price, the burden of proof is on the bull.

Market multiples corroborate the caution. Retail REITs trade above mid‑cycle averages, and SPG itself sits rich on several measures: about 24.9× earnings (69th percentile), 10.0× sales (72nd), and 19.2× book (90th). Price‑to‑book is less helpful here given historic‑cost accounting, but a reasonable reset to roughly 21× earnings and 8.5× sales triangulates to US$145–US$160—a range that chimes with the DCF.

Two near‑term checkpoints could close the gap between hope and reality. First, full‑year 2025 results and 2026 guidance, expected in late February 2026, should anchor growth nearer 4.5% and margins around 39%. If that happens, I expect the market to take the premium down a notch, consistent with a move toward the mid‑US$160s to high‑US$150s. Second, redevelopment milestones through 2026 should confirm earlier stabilisation, which shortens duration and chips away at valuation support.

Of course, there are ways I could be wrong on the downside. Stronger leasing spreads, faster project stabilisation, or a lower discount rate would lift fair value. If growth trends closer to 5.2% and margins toward 44–45%, I could justify values from the high US$170s to high US$190s, which would challenge a Sell call. The bear case runs the other way: slower leasing, more dilution from international ventures, and a more capital‑intensive pipeline push value down toward US$113.

What will I watch? Three things. First, leasing spreads and the volume of leased‑but‑not‑open space; the former signals pricing power, the latter the pace to cash. Second, property‑tax and utilities lines; if they cool, margin pressure eases. Third, the cadence and returns of redevelopments and international JVs; that is where real upside could emerge if execution beats history.

Stepping back, Simon is a superb franchise with prime centres, sticky tenants, and an investment‑grade balance sheet. None of that is in doubt. The issue is the price. From US$182, the shares assume more growth, more margin, and more time than I can underwrite. Until guidance and milestones reset expectations, I see better risk‑reward elsewhere. I will avoid over the next 12 months and revisit after the 2026 outlook is on the table.

[Simon Property Group shares are overvalued.](https://valuationbot.ai/blog/why-i-d-sell-simon-property-group-at-us-182) At US$182 a share, the market bakes in faster growth, fatter margins, and a longer runway than I think the assets can deliver. ## **Investment thesis**

Simon Property Group is priced for perfection. At US$182 a share, the market bakes in faster growth, fatter margins, and a longer runway than I think the assets can deliver. My base‑case value is US$152 per share, which points to 12–22% downside from here.

The gap starts with what today’s price implies. To justify this level, you need roughly 5.2% revenue growth, a 44.7% long‑run net margin, and an 11‑year glide path to stability. I assume 4.5% growth, a 39% steady‑state margin, and ten years to stability. The difference may look small on paper, but over a decade it compounds into a large value gap.

The operational ceiling is already in sight. Occupancy sits near 96%, which limits scope for a step‑change in rent growth. Base minimum rent runs at about US$59 per square foot and escalators add steady, not explosive, uplift. Meanwhile, property operating costs and taxes keep grinding higher, which crimps the scope for margin expansion from here. On the current footprint, that mix points to mid‑single‑digit growth and a net margin that settles closer to 39% than 45%.

Unit economics back this up. Management’s own data imply operating costs around US$10.60 per square foot per year and an NOI margin in the low 60s—healthy, but hardly the stuff of further operating‑leverage miracles. When a portfolio is this mature, the heavy lifting comes from lease roll‑over and redevelopment, not from squeezing more out of day‑to‑day operations.

Duration is the other over‑reach. The shares embed an 11‑year runway; I think most large projects will be substantially stabilised by 2026, which argues for a shorter, ten‑year path back to steady state. A shorter runway lowers duration premia in any sensible model and trims fair value.

My DCF tells a consistent story. The base case lands at US$152 per share. Simulated outcomes cluster tightly: the 25th to 75th percentiles sit between US$142 and US$161, and even the 90th and 95th percentiles—US$170 and US$176—sit below today’s price. When your upside cases fail to clear the screen price, the burden of proof is on the bull.

Market multiples corroborate the caution. Retail REITs trade above mid‑cycle averages, and SPG itself sits rich on several measures: about 24.9× earnings (69th percentile), 10.0× sales (72nd), and 19.2× book (90th). Price‑to‑book is less helpful here given historic‑cost accounting, but a reasonable reset to roughly 21× earnings and 8.5× sales triangulates to US$145–US$160—a range that chimes with the DCF.

Two near‑term checkpoints could close the gap between hope and reality. First, full‑year 2025 results and 2026 guidance, expected in late February 2026, should anchor growth nearer 4.5% and margins around 39%. If that happens, I expect the market to take the premium down a notch, consistent with a move toward the mid‑US$160s to high‑US$150s. Second, redevelopment milestones through 2026 should confirm earlier stabilisation, which shortens duration and chips away at valuation support.

Of course, there are ways I could be wrong on the downside. Stronger leasing spreads, faster project stabilisation, or a lower discount rate would lift fair value. If growth trends closer to 5.2% and margins toward 44–45%, I could justify values from the high US$170s to high US$190s, which would challenge a Sell call. The bear case runs the other way: slower leasing, more dilution from international ventures, and a more capital‑intensive pipeline push value down toward US$113.

What will I watch? Three things. First, leasing spreads and the volume of leased‑but‑not‑open space; the former signals pricing power, the latter the pace to cash. Second, property‑tax and utilities lines; if they cool, margin pressure eases. Third, the cadence and returns of redevelopments and international JVs; that is where real upside could emerge if execution beats history.

Stepping back, Simon is a superb franchise with prime centres, sticky tenants, and an investment‑grade balance sheet. None of that is in doubt. The issue is the price. From US$182, the shares assume more growth, more margin, and more time than I can underwrite. Until guidance and milestones reset expectations, I see better risk‑reward elsewhere. I will avoid over the next 12 months and revisit after the 2026 outlook is on the table.

[Simon Property Group shares are overvalued.](https://valuationbot.ai/blog/why-i-d-sell-simon-property-group-at-us-182) At US$182 a share, the market bakes in faster growth, fatter margins, and a longer runway than I think the assets can deliver. ## **Executive summary**

* **Company:** Simon Property Group, Inc.
* **Ticker:** [$SPG](/quote/SPG/)

## **Investment thesis**

Simon Property Group is priced for perfection. At US$182 a share, the market bakes in faster growth, fatter margins, and a longer runway than I think the assets can deliver. My base‑case value is US$152 per share, which points to 12–22% downside from here.

The gap starts with what today’s price implies. To justify this level, you need roughly 5.2% revenue growth, a 44.7% long‑run net margin, and an 11‑year glide path to stability. I assume 4.5% growth, a 39% steady‑state margin, and ten years to stability. The difference may look small on paper, but over a decade it compounds into a large value gap.

The operational ceiling is already in sight. Occupancy sits near 96%, which limits scope for a step‑change in rent growth. Base minimum rent runs at about US$59 per square foot and escalators add steady, not explosive, uplift. Meanwhile, property operating costs and taxes keep grinding higher, which crimps the scope for margin expansion from here. On the current footprint, that mix points to mid‑single‑digit growth and a net margin that settles closer to 39% than 45%.

Unit economics back this up. Management’s own data imply operating costs around US$10.60 per square foot per year and an NOI margin in the low 60s—healthy, but hardly the stuff of further operating‑leverage miracles. When a portfolio is this mature, the heavy lifting comes from lease roll‑over and redevelopment, not from squeezing more out of day‑to‑day operations.

Duration is the other over‑reach. The shares embed an 11‑year runway; I think most large projects will be substantially stabilised by 2026, which argues for a shorter, ten‑year path back to steady state. A shorter runway lowers duration premia in any sensible model and trims fair value.

My DCF tells a consistent story. The base case lands at US$152 per share. Simulated outcomes cluster tightly: the 25th to 75th percentiles sit between US$142 and US$161, and even the 90th and 95th percentiles—US$170 and US$176—sit below today’s price. When your upside cases fail to clear the screen price, the burden of proof is on the bull.

Market multiples corroborate the caution. Retail REITs trade above mid‑cycle averages, and SPG itself sits rich on several measures: about 24.9× earnings (69th percentile), 10.0× sales (72nd), and 19.2× book (90th). Price‑to‑book is less helpful here given historic‑cost accounting, but a reasonable reset to roughly 21× earnings and 8.5× sales triangulates to US$145–US$160—a range that chimes with the DCF.

Two near‑term checkpoints could close the gap between hope and reality. First, full‑year 2025 results and 2026 guidance, expected in late February 2026, should anchor growth nearer 4.5% and margins around 39%. If that happens, I expect the market to take the premium down a notch, consistent with a move toward the mid‑US$160s to high‑US$150s. Second, redevelopment milestones through 2026 should confirm earlier stabilisation, which shortens duration and chips away at valuation support.

Of course, there are ways I could be wrong on the downside. Stronger leasing spreads, faster project stabilisation, or a lower discount rate would lift fair value. If growth trends closer to 5.2% and margins toward 44–45%, I could justify values from the high US$170s to high US$190s, which would challenge a Sell call. The bear case runs the other way: slower leasing, more dilution from international ventures, and a more capital‑intensive pipeline push value down toward US$113.

What will I watch? Three things. First, leasing spreads and the volume of leased‑but‑not‑open space; the former signals pricing power, the latter the pace to cash. Second, property‑tax and utilities lines; if they cool, margin pressure eases. Third, the cadence and returns of redevelopments and international JVs; that is where real upside could emerge if execution beats history.

Stepping back, Simon is a superb franchise with prime centres, sticky tenants, and an investment‑grade balance sheet. None of that is in doubt. The issue is the price. From US$182, the shares assume more growth, more margin, and more time than I can underwrite. Until guidance and milestones reset expectations, I see better risk‑reward elsewhere. I will avoid over the next 12 months and revisit after the 2026 outlook is on the table.

## Why I’d Sell Simon Property Group at US$182

[Simon Property Group shares are overvalued.](https://valuationbot.ai/blog/why-i-d-sell-simon-property-group-at-us-182) At US$182 a share, the market bakes in faster growth, fatter margins, and a longer runway than I think the assets can deliver. My base‑case value is US$152 per share, which points to 12–22% downside from here, so I would sell.

--

## **Executive summary**

* **Company:** Simon Property Group, Inc.
* **Ticker:** [$SPG](/quote/SPG/)
* **What I'm doing:** Avoiding
* **Current price:** US$182.07
* **Estimated value:** US$152.38
* **Upside:** -16.3%
* **Expected IRR:** 6.5%

--

## **Investment thesis**

Simon Property Group is priced for perfection. At US$182 a share, the market bakes in faster growth, fatter margins, and a longer runway than I think the assets can deliver. My base‑case value is US$152 per share, which points to 12–22% downside from here.

The gap starts with what today’s price implies. To justify this level, you need roughly 5.2% revenue growth, a 44.7% long‑run net margin, and an 11‑year glide path to stability. I assume 4.5% growth, a 39% steady‑state margin, and ten years to stability. The difference may look small on paper, but over a decade it compounds into a large value gap.

The operational ceiling is already in sight. Occupancy sits near 96%, which limits scope for a step‑change in rent growth. Base minimum rent runs at about US$59 per square foot and escalators add steady, not explosive, uplift. Meanwhile, property operating costs and taxes keep grinding higher, which crimps the scope for margin expansion from here. On the current footprint, that mix points to mid‑single‑digit growth and a net margin that settles closer to 39% than 45%.

Unit economics back this up. Management’s own data imply operating costs around US$10.60 per square foot per year and an NOI margin in the low 60s—healthy, but hardly the stuff of further operating‑leverage miracles. When a portfolio is this mature, the heavy lifting comes from lease roll‑over and redevelopment, not from squeezing more out of day‑to‑day operations.

Duration is the other over‑reach. The shares embed an 11‑year runway; I think most large projects will be substantially stabilised by 2026, which argues for a shorter, ten‑year path back to steady state. A shorter runway lowers duration premia in any sensible model and trims fair value.

My DCF tells a consistent story. The base case lands at US$152 per share. Simulated outcomes cluster tightly: the 25th to 75th percentiles sit between US$142 and US$161, and even the 90th and 95th percentiles—US$170 and US$176—sit below today’s price. When your upside cases fail to clear the screen price, the burden of proof is on the bull.

Market multiples corroborate the caution. Retail REITs trade above mid‑cycle averages, and SPG itself sits rich on several measures: about 24.9× earnings (69th percentile), 10.0× sales (72nd), and 19.2× book (90th). Price‑to‑book is less helpful here given historic‑cost accounting, but a reasonable reset to roughly 21× earnings and 8.5× sales triangulates to US$145–US$160—a range that chimes with the DCF.

Two near‑term checkpoints could close the gap between hope and reality. First, full‑year 2025 results and 2026 guidance, expected in late February 2026, should anchor growth nearer 4.5% and margins around 39%. If that happens, I expect the market to take the premium down a notch, consistent with a move toward the mid‑US$160s to high‑US$150s. Second, redevelopment milestones through 2026 should confirm earlier stabilisation, which shortens duration and chips away at valuation support.

Of course, there are ways I could be wrong on the downside. Stronger leasing spreads, faster project stabilisation, or a lower discount rate would lift fair value. If growth trends closer to 5.2% and margins toward 44–45%, I could justify values from the high US$170s to high US$190s, which would challenge a Sell call. The bear case runs the other way: slower leasing, more dilution from international ventures, and a more capital‑intensive pipeline push value down toward US$113.

What will I watch? Three things. First, leasing spreads and the volume of leased‑but‑not‑open space; the former signals pricing power, the latter the pace to cash. Second, property‑tax and utilities lines; if they cool, margin pressure eases. Third, the cadence and returns of redevelopments and international JVs; that is where real upside could emerge if execution beats history.

Stepping back, Simon is a superb franchise with prime centres, sticky tenants, and an investment‑grade balance sheet. None of that is in doubt. The issue is the price. From US$182, the shares assume more growth, more margin, and more time than I can underwrite. Until guidance and milestones reset expectations, I see better risk‑reward elsewhere. I will avoid over the next 12 months and revisit after the 2026 outlook is on the table.

* ### Dividend yield above industry average

  Simon Property Group Inc., based in Indianapolis, is a retail REIT that is one of the largest owners of high-end malls, outlet centers, and lifestyle destinations in North America, Asia, and Europe. In 2016, the company had expanded its profile by investing in the retail operations of several well-known retail brands, including Reebok, Aeropostale, Nautica, and Forever 21 through its partnerships, including SPARC and ABG. The investments were reconsidered after the pandemic, once consumers began to return to outdoor retail spaces. In 2023, the company began to sell its interest in retail brands and in 2024, Simon sold its remaining interest in ABG brands. The company still has active joint venture interests including an 84% interest in the Taubman Group, a 22% interest in Klepierre, a Paris-based real estate firm, and SPARC. SPG also operates Simon Brand Ventures, which offers appraisals and real estate services.
  At the end of 2024, Simon owned or had interests in about 233 properties with about 12 million square feet of international leasable space and 170 million square feet of domestic space. ## **Investment thesis**

Simon Property Group is priced for perfection. At US$182 a share, the market bakes in faster growth, fatter margins, and a longer runway than I think the assets can deliver. My base‑case value is US$152 per share, which points to 12–22% downside from here.

The gap starts with what today’s price implies. To justify this level, you need roughly 5.2% revenue growth, a 44.7% long‑run net margin, and an 11‑year glide path to stability. I assume 4.5% growth, a 39% steady‑state margin, and ten years to stability. The difference may look small on paper, but over a decade it compounds into a large value gap.

The operational ceiling is already in sight. Occupancy sits near 96%, which limits scope for a step‑change in rent growth. Base minimum rent runs at about US$59 per square foot and escalators add steady, not explosive, uplift. Meanwhile, property operating costs and taxes keep grinding higher, which crimps the scope for margin expansion from here. On the current footprint, that mix points to mid‑single‑digit growth and a net margin that settles closer to 39% than 45%.

Unit economics back this up. Management’s own data imply operating costs around US$10.60 per square foot per year and an NOI margin in the low 60s—healthy, but hardly the stuff of further operating‑leverage miracles. When a portfolio is this mature, the heavy lifting comes from lease roll‑over and redevelopment, not from squeezing more out of day‑to‑day operations.

Duration is the other over‑reach. The shares embed an 11‑year runway; I think most large projects will be substantially stabilised by 2026, which argues for a shorter, ten‑year path back to steady state. A shorter runway lowers duration premia in any sensible model and trims fair value.

My DCF tells a consistent story. The base case lands at US$152 per share. Simulated outcomes cluster tightly: the 25th to 75th percentiles sit between US$142 and US$161, and even the 90th and 95th percentiles—US$170 and US$176—sit below today’s price. When your upside cases fail to clear the screen price, the burden of proof is on the bull.

Market multiples corroborate the caution. Retail REITs trade above mid‑cycle averages, and SPG itself sits rich on several measures: about 24.9× earnings (69th percentile), 10.0× sales (72nd), and 19.2× book (90th). Price‑to‑book is less helpful here given historic‑cost accounting, but a reasonable reset to roughly 21× earnings and 8.5× sales triangulates to US$145–US$160—a range that chimes with the DCF.

Two near‑term checkpoints could close the gap between hope and reality. First, full‑year 2025 results and 2026 guidance, expected in late February 2026, should anchor growth nearer 4.5% and margins around 39%. If that happens, I expect the market to take the premium down a notch, consistent with a move toward the mid‑US$160s to high‑US$150s. Second, redevelopment milestones through 2026 should confirm earlier stabilisation, which shortens duration and chips away at valuation support.

Of course, there are ways I could be wrong on the downside. Stronger leasing spreads, faster project stabilisation, or a lower discount rate would lift fair value. If growth trends closer to 5.2% and margins toward 44–45%, I could justify values from the high US$170s to high US$190s, which would challenge a Sell call. The bear case runs the other way: slower leasing, more dilution from international ventures, and a more capital‑intensive pipeline push value down toward US$113.

What will I watch? Three things. First, leasing spreads and the volume of leased‑but‑not‑open space; the former signals pricing power, the latter the pace to cash. Second, property‑tax and utilities lines; if they cool, margin pressure eases. Third, the cadence and returns of redevelopments and international JVs; that is where real upside could emerge if execution beats history.

Stepping back, Simon is a superb franchise with prime centres, sticky tenants, and an investment‑grade balance sheet. None of that is in doubt. The issue is the price. From US$182, the shares assume more growth, more margin, and more time than I can underwrite. Until guidance and milestones reset expectations, I see better risk‑reward elsewhere. I will avoid over the next 12 months and revisit after the 2026 outlook is on the table.

## **Investment thesis**

Simon Property Group is priced for perfection. At US$182 a share, the market bakes in faster growth, fatter margins, and a longer runway than I think the assets can deliver. My base‑case value is US$152 per share, which points to 12–22% downside from here.

The gap starts with what today’s price implies. To justify this level, you need roughly 5.2% revenue growth, a 44.7% long‑run net margin, and an 11‑year glide path to stability. I assume 4.5% growth, a 39% steady‑state margin, and ten years to stability. The difference may look small on paper, but over a decade it compounds into a large value gap.

The operational ceiling is already in sight. Occupancy sits near 96%, which limits scope for a step‑change in rent growth. Base minimum rent runs at about US$59 per square foot and escalators add steady, not explosive, uplift. Meanwhile, property operating costs and taxes keep grinding higher, which crimps the scope for margin expansion from here. On the current footprint, that mix points to mid‑single‑digit growth and a net margin that settles closer to 39% than 45%.

Unit economics back this up. Management’s own data imply operating costs around US$10.60 per square foot per year and an NOI margin in the low 60s—healthy, but hardly the stuff of further operating‑leverage miracles. When a portfolio is this mature, the heavy lifting comes from lease roll‑over and redevelopment, not from squeezing more out of day‑to‑day operations.

Duration is the other over‑reach. The shares embed an 11‑year runway; I think most large projects will be substantially stabilised by 2026, which argues for a shorter, ten‑year path back to steady state. A shorter runway lowers duration premia in any sensible model and trims fair value.

My DCF tells a consistent story. The base case lands at US$152 per share. Simulated outcomes cluster tightly: the 25th to 75th percentiles sit between US$142 and US$161, and even the 90th and 95th percentiles—US$170 and US$176—sit below today’s price. When your upside cases fail to clear the screen price, the burden of proof is on the bull.

Market multiples corroborate the caution. Retail REITs trade above mid‑cycle averages, and SPG itself sits rich on several measures: about 24.9× earnings (69th percentile), 10.0× sales (72nd), and 19.2× book (90th). Price‑to‑book is less helpful here given historic‑cost accounting, but a reasonable reset to roughly 21× earnings and 8.5× sales triangulates to US$145–US$160—a range that chimes with the DCF.

Two near‑term checkpoints could close the gap between hope and reality. First, full‑year 2025 results and 2026 guidance, expected in late February 2026, should anchor growth nearer 4.5% and margins around 39%. If that happens, I expect the market to take the premium down a notch, consistent with a move toward the mid‑US$160s to high‑US$150s. Second, redevelopment milestones through 2026 should confirm earlier stabilisation, which shortens duration and chips away at valuation support.

Of course, there are ways I could be wrong on the downside. Stronger leasing spreads, faster project stabilisation, or a lower discount rate would lift fair value. If growth trends closer to 5.2% and margins toward 44–45%, I could justify values from the high US$170s to high US$190s, which would challenge a Sell call. The bear case runs the other way: slower leasing, more dilution from international ventures, and a more capital‑intensive pipeline push value down toward US$113.

What will I watch? Three things. First, leasing spreads and the volume of leased‑but‑not‑open space; the former signals pricing power, the latter the pace to cash. Second, property‑tax and utilities lines; if they cool, margin pressure eases. Third, the cadence and returns of redevelopments and international JVs; that is where real upside could emerge if execution beats history.

Stepping back, Simon is a superb franchise with prime centres, sticky tenants, and an investment‑grade balance sheet. None of that is in doubt. The issue is the price. From US$182, the shares assume more growth, more margin, and more time than I can underwrite. Until guidance and milestones reset expectations, I see better risk‑reward elsewhere. I will avoid over the next 12 months and revisit after the 2026 outlook is on the table.

## **Investment thesis**

Simon Property Group is priced for perfection. At US$182 a share, the market bakes in faster growth, fatter margins, and a longer runway than I think the assets can deliver. My base‑case value is US$152 per share, which points to 12–22% downside from here.

The gap starts with what today’s price implies. To justify this level, you need roughly 5.2% revenue growth, a 44.7% long‑run net margin, and an 11‑year glide path to stability. I assume 4.5% growth, a 39% steady‑state margin, and ten years to stability. The difference may look small on paper, but over a decade it compounds into a large value gap.

The operational ceiling is already in sight. Occupancy sits near 96%, which limits scope for a step‑change in rent growth. Base minimum rent runs at about US$59 per square foot and escalators add steady, not explosive, uplift. Meanwhile, property operating costs and taxes keep grinding higher, which crimps the scope for margin expansion from here. On the current footprint, that mix points to mid‑single‑digit growth and a net margin that settles closer to 39% than 45%.

Unit economics back this up. Management’s own data imply operating costs around US$10.60 per square foot per year and an NOI margin in the low 60s—healthy, but hardly the stuff of further operating‑leverage miracles. When a portfolio is this mature, the heavy lifting comes from lease roll‑over and redevelopment, not from squeezing more out of day‑to‑day operations.

Duration is the other over‑reach. The shares embed an 11‑year runway; I think most large projects will be substantially stabilised by 2026, which argues for a shorter, ten‑year path back to steady state. A shorter runway lowers duration premia in any sensible model and trims fair value.

My DCF tells a consistent story. The base case lands at US$152 per share. Simulated outcomes cluster tightly: the 25th to 75th percentiles sit between US$142 and US$161, and even the 90th and 95th percentiles—US$170 and US$176—sit below today’s price. When your upside cases fail to clear the screen price, the burden of proof is on the bull.

Market multiples corroborate the caution. Retail REITs trade above mid‑cycle averages, and SPG itself sits rich on several measures: about 24.9× earnings (69th percentile), 10.0× sales (72nd), and 19.2× book (90th). Price‑to‑book is less helpful here given historic‑cost accounting, but a reasonable reset to roughly 21× earnings and 8.5× sales triangulates to US$145–US$160—a range that chimes with the DCF.

Two near‑term checkpoints could close the gap between hope and reality. First, full‑year 2025 results and 2026 guidance, expected in late February 2026, should anchor growth nearer 4.5% and margins around 39%. If that happens, I expect the market to take the premium down a notch, consistent with a move toward the mid‑US$160s to high‑US$150s. Second, redevelopment milestones through 2026 should confirm earlier stabilisation, which shortens duration and chips away at valuation support.

Of course, there are ways I could be wrong on the downside. Stronger leasing spreads, faster project stabilisation, or a lower discount rate would lift fair value. If growth trends closer to 5.2% and margins toward 44–45%, I could justify values from the high US$170s to high US$190s, which would challenge a Sell call. The bear case runs the other way: slower leasing, more dilution from international ventures, and a more capital‑intensive pipeline push value down toward US$113.

What will I watch? Three things. First, leasing spreads and the volume of leased‑but‑not‑open space; the former signals pricing power, the latter the pace to cash. Second, property‑tax and utilities lines; if they cool, margin pressure eases. Third, the cadence and returns of redevelopments and international JVs; that is where real upside could emerge if execution beats history.

Stepping back, Simon is a superb franchise with prime centres, sticky tenants, and an investment‑grade balance sheet. None of that is in doubt. The issue is the price. From US$182, the shares assume more growth, more margin, and more time than I can underwrite. Until guidance and milestones reset expectations, I see better risk‑reward elsewhere. I will avoid over the next 12 months and revisit after the 2026 outlook is on the table.

In 2016, the company had expanded its profile by investing in the retail operations of several well-known retail brands, including Reebok, Aeropostale, Nautica, and Forever 21 through its partnerships, including SPARC and ABG. In 2023, the company began to sell its interest in retail brands and in 2024, Simon sold its remaining interest in ABG brands. The company still has active joint venture interests including an 84% interest in the Taubman Group, a 22% interest in Klepierre, a Paris-based real estate firm, and SPARC. SPG also operates Simon Brand Ventures, which offers appraisals and real estate services.
  At the end of 2024, Simon owned or had interests in about 233 properties with about 12 million square feet of international leasable space and 170 million square feet of domestic space. Last year, revenues were just under $6 billion, of which about 60% were from joint venture interest. At the end of 1Q25, about 91% of portfolio NOI was from US assets including The Mills. Of domestic NOI, over 40% is from properties in portfolio-heavy Texas, California, and Florida. The REIT has a varied tenant base. Beginning 2025, its largest domestic tenants were Gap Inc., Tapestry, and Knitwell, although the GAP only accounts for less than 3% of total base minimum rent. SPG is a member of the S&P 500 and has a market cap is about $67.8 billion.

  Simon Property Group Inc., based in Indianapolis, is a retail REIT that is one of the largest owners of high-end malls, outlet centers, and lifestyle destinations in North America, Asia, and Europe. In 2016, the company had expanded its profile by investing in the retail operations of several well-known retail brands, including Reebok, Aeropostale, Nautica, and Forever 21 through its partnerships, including SPARC and ABG. The investments were reconsidered after the pandemic, once consumers began to return to outdoor retail spaces.
